title: George Washington Carver and the Peanut Plant
summary: How George Washington Carver, an agricultural scientist born into slavery, helped farmers heal tired soil with crop rotation and found hundreds of new uses for the peanut plant.
poll: Helping the environment and helping people can be the same goal.

versions.title: George Washington Carver and the Peanut Plant
versions.text:
Carver was a great scientist. He lived long ago. He was born a slave. His home was in Missouri.

He loved plants. He liked to see them grow. He went to school to learn more.

Later, he worked at a school. The school was in Alabama. He helped farmers there.

Many farmers grew just cotton. They grew it year after year. This made the soil tired. The soil could not grow good crops.

Carver had an idea. Grow peanuts, too! Peanuts helped the tired soil grow strong again.

Then farmers grew lots of peanuts. But what could they do with them all?

Carver found out. He found many uses for the peanut. He made foods. He made soap. He made other things, too.

He helped poor farmers for years. He died in 1943.

Today, we call him a great scientist. He helped the soil. He helped farmers, too.

versions.title: George Washington Carver and the Peanut Plant
versions.text:
More than one hundred fifty years ago, around the year 1864, George Washington Carver was born into slavery on a small farm in the state of Missouri. Despite this extremely difficult start in life, he grew up to become one of the most celebrated and pioneering scientists in the entire history of American agriculture.

As a child, Carver was fascinated by plants and spent countless hours observing how they grew in the woods surrounding his home, teaching himself to identify and care for nearly every plant he encountered there. He was determined to learn everything he possibly could about the natural world, so as a young man he traveled far from home to attend college, eventually earning an advanced degree in agricultural science at a time when few people expected such an achievement from someone of his background.

As an adult, Carver went to work at a school in Alabama called Tuskegee Institute. There, he devoted his entire career to pioneering agricultural research aimed at helping poor farmers, many of them formerly enslaved people and their children, grow healthier crops and earn a far more stable living from their land. He even built a mobile classroom on a wagon so he could bring his conservation lessons directly to farmers who could not travel to the school.

At that time, many Southern farmers grew only a single crop, cotton, year after year on the exact same fields. Growing the very same crop repeatedly wore out the soil, steadily draining it of the nutrients that plants genuinely require, so the land eventually could no longer produce good harvests, a problem Carver recognized demanded real soil conservation.

Carver, ever resourceful, proposed a practical and sustainable solution known as crop rotation. He urged farmers to alternate cotton with peanuts, sweet potatoes, and other plants that could return essential nutrients to the exhausted soil, helping it grow strong and productive once again in a genuinely sustainable way, and he often traveled directly to farms to teach these conservation methods in person.

Soon, many farmers who adopted this rotation plan were growing large quantities of peanuts. But a new problem quickly appeared: what could anyone possibly do with so many extra peanuts?

Carver's research provided a remarkably versatile answer. Through years of patient, careful experiments in his laboratory, he made discovery after discovery, eventually finding hundreds of different and versatile uses for the peanut plant, including foods, soap, dyes, inks, cosmetics, and many other useful products, along with additional uses for sweet potatoes and soybeans.

Carver spent his entire life helping farmers and conducting pioneering agricultural research, and national organizations recognized his scientific contributions both during his lifetime and long after his death in 1943. Today, people around the country still honor his resourceful discoveries and his remarkable generosity.

versions.title: George Washington Carver and the Peanut Plant
versions.text:
More than a century and a half ago, around the year 1864, George Washington Carver was born into slavery on a small farm in the state of Missouri. Despite this extraordinarily difficult start in life, he matured into one of the most celebrated and pioneering scientists in the entire history of American agriculture.

As a child, Carver was fascinated by plants and spent countless hours observing how they grew in the woods surrounding his home, patiently teaching himself to identify and care for nearly every plant species he encountered there. He was determined to learn everything he possibly could about the natural world, so as a young man he traveled far from home to attend college, eventually earning an advanced degree in agricultural science at a time when few people anticipated such an achievement from someone of his background.

As an adult, Carver went to work at an institution in Alabama called Tuskegee Institute. There, he devoted his entire career to pioneering agricultural research aimed at assisting impoverished farmers, many of them formerly enslaved people and their descendants, in growing healthier crops and earning a far more stable living from their land. He even constructed a mobile classroom mounted on a wagon so he could bring his conservation lessons directly to farmers who could not afford to travel to the institute.

At that time, many Southern farmers cultivated only a single crop, cotton, year after year on the exact same fields. Growing the very same crop repeatedly exhausted the soil, steadily draining it of the nutrients that plants genuinely require, so the land eventually could no longer produce adequate harvests, a problem Carver recognized demanded genuine soil conservation.

Carver, ever resourceful, proposed a practical and sustainable solution known as crop rotation. He urged farmers to alternate cotton with peanuts, sweet potatoes, and other plants capable of returning essential nutrients to the exhausted soil, helping it grow strong and productive once more in a genuinely sustainable manner, and he frequently traveled directly to farms to teach these conservation methods in person.

Soon, many farmers who adopted this rotation plan were cultivating substantial quantities of peanuts. But a new difficulty quickly emerged: what could anyone possibly do with so many surplus peanuts?

Carver's research furnished a remarkably versatile answer. Through years of patient, meticulous experiments conducted in his laboratory, he made discovery after discovery, eventually identifying hundreds of different and versatile uses for the peanut plant, including foods, soap, dyes, inks, cosmetics, and numerous other useful products, along with additional uses for sweet potatoes and soybeans.

versions.title: George Washington Carver and the Peanut Plant
versions.text:
More than a full century and a half ago, around the year 1864, George Washington Carver was born into slavery on a small farm in the state of Missouri. Despite this extraordinarily difficult and constrained start in life, he gradually matured into one of the most celebrated and pioneering scientists in the entire history of American agriculture.

As a child, Carver was deeply fascinated by plants and spent countless hours observing how they grew in the woods surrounding his home, patiently teaching himself to identify and care for nearly every plant species he encountered there. He was determined to learn everything he possibly could about the natural world, so as a young man he traveled far from home to attend college, eventually earning an advanced degree in agricultural science at a time when exceedingly few people anticipated such an achievement from someone of his background.

As an adult, Carver went to work at an institution in Alabama called Tuskegee Institute. There, he devoted his entire career to pioneering agricultural research aimed at assisting impoverished farmers, many of them formerly enslaved people and their descendants, in growing healthier crops and earning a far more stable livelihood from their land. He even constructed a mobile classroom mounted upon a wagon so that he could bring his conservation lessons directly to farmers who could not otherwise afford to travel to the institute.

At that time, many Southern farmers cultivated only a single crop, cotton, year after year on the exact same fields. Growing the very same crop repeatedly and relentlessly exhausted the soil, steadily draining it of the nutrients that plants genuinely require, so the land eventually could no longer produce adequate harvests, a problem Carver recognized demanded genuine, lasting soil conservation.

Carver, ever resourceful, proposed a practical and sustainable solution known as crop rotation. He urged farmers to alternate cotton with peanuts, sweet potatoes, and other plants capable of returning essential nutrients to the thoroughly exhausted soil, helping it grow strong and productive once more in a genuinely sustainable manner, and he frequently traveled directly to farms himself to teach these conservation methods in person.

Soon, many farmers who adopted this rotation plan were cultivating substantial quantities of peanuts. But a new difficulty quickly emerged: what could anyone possibly do with so many surplus peanuts?

Carver's research ultimately furnished a remarkably versatile answer. Through years of patient, meticulous experiments conducted within his modest laboratory, he made discovery after discovery, eventually identifying literally hundreds of different and versatile uses for the peanut plant, including foods, soap, dyes, inks, cosmetics, and numerous other useful products, along with additional uses for sweet potatoes and soybeans.

Carver devoted his entire life to assisting farmers and conducting pioneering agricultural research, and national organizations recognized his scientific contributions both during his lifetime and long afterward, following his death in 1943. questions.why: Traveling directly to farms let Carver reach farmers who could not afford to travel to the institute themselves.

wrong.A: The article does not suggest he disliked the classroom.
wrong.B: The article does not say he was banned from the school.
wrong.C: The article does not mention farmers paying him.

questions.stem: Why do you think Carver's research into hundreds of peanut uses mattered so much to farmers?
options: It made all peanuts illegal to waste
It made cotton farming popular again
It gave farmers reasons to keep growing peanuts
It was strictly required by the government of the country
questions.why: Finding many uses for peanuts gave farmers real reasons to keep growing a crop that also helped restore their soil.

wrong.A: The article does not mention any law about waste.
wrong.B: The research supported peanuts and sweet potatoes, not cotton.
wrong.D: The article does not mention a government requirement.

questions.stem: Why does the author include details about Carver's difficult childhood, including being born into slavery?
options: To explain the full geography of Missouri
To show how far he rose despite a hard beginning
To compare him fairly to other farmers
To give a history lesson unrelated to his science
questions.why: Including his difficult start helps readers appreciate how remarkable his later achievements in science truly were.

wrong.A: The article gives almost no geography of Missouri.
wrong.C: No other farmers are compared to him here.
wrong.D: This detail connects directly to his later scientific achievements.

MID.prompt: Explain how Carver's crop rotation idea could still help farmers today. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained Carver's crop rotation idea.
I used at least two details from the article.
I connected his idea to farming today.
MID.modelAnswer: Carver's idea of crop rotation could still help farmers today because growing different plants, like peanuts and sweet potatoes, instead of the same crop every year keeps putting good nutrients back into the soil. He also showed that research into new uses for a crop, like the hundreds of uses he found for peanuts, can give farmers more reasons and markets to grow soil-friendly plants instead of crops that wear out the land.

keyWords.definition: good at finding clever ways to solve problems with what is available
keyWords.example: The resourceful hikers used a branch to fix the broken tent pole.

keyWords.definition: able to continue over a long time without running out or causing harm
keyWords.example: The school started a sustainable recycling program that has lasted for years.

keyWords.definition: being among the first to try or develop something new
keyWords.example: Her pioneering research changed how scientists study ocean currents.

keyWords.definition: the careful protection and management of something valuable, such as soil, water, or wildlife
keyWords.example: The park rangers taught us about water conservation during the drought.

keyWords.definition: able to be used for many different purposes
keyWords.example: A versatile tool like a multi-use knife can cut, open cans, and more.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Carver's fame rests mainly on his difficult childhood.
Carver was a pioneering scientist whose research transformed the peanut.
Carver's only lasting contribution was the mobile classroom wagon.
Carver's methods were quickly forgotten after his death.
questions.why: The article traces his pioneering soil conservation methods and his versatile discoveries about peanut uses.

wrong.A: His childhood is background; his science is the article's focus.
wrong.C: The wagon is one detail among many of his contributions.
wrong.D: People still honor him today, so his work was not forgotten.

questions.stem: According to the article, what problem with cotton farming made Carver's crop rotation method necessary?
options: Cotton was much too expensive to buy
Cotton attracted too many insects
Cotton could not be sold outside the South
Repeated cotton planting exhausted the soil
questions.why: In the article, growing cotton repeatedly drained the soil of the nutrients plants need.

wrong.A: Cost is not mentioned as the problem.
wrong.B: Insects are not mentioned in the article.
wrong.C: Selling cotton outside the South is not mentioned.

questions.stem: How did Carver bring his conservation lessons directly to farmers?

He built a new laboratory building

He opened a large university campus

wrong.C: A newspaper is not mentioned.

questions.stem: The article describes Carver's many uses for the peanut as versatile. What does versatile mean here?
options: Expensive, rare, and hard to find
Difficult to understand fully
Able to be used in many different ways
Limited to just one single purpose and use

wrong.A: Cost and rarity are not what versatile means.
wrong.B: Versatile does not mean difficult.
wrong.D: Versatile is the opposite of being limited to one purpose.

questions.stem: What can you infer from Carver's choice to call his crop rotation approach sustainable?
options: He expected farmers to abandon it quickly
He believed cotton was a better long-term crop for the soil
He thought peanuts should replace cotton and
He wanted the soil to produce well for a very long time
questions.why: Calling the method sustainable shows Carver cared about the soil remaining productive for many years, not just a single season.

wrong.A: This contradicts the idea of a lasting, sustainable method.
wrong.B: The article shows cotton farming was the problem, not the long-term solution.
wrong.C: The article describes rotating crops, not fully replacing cotton.

questions.stem: Why most likely did national organizations recognize Carver's scientific contributions?
options: His research had a lasting, practical impact on farming and soil health
He was closely related to important government officials in Alabama
He was the only agricultural scientist in the whole country
His work was limited to just a single small Alabama county
questions.why: Recognition both during and after his life suggests his research had a lasting, practical effect on farming and soil health.

wrong.B: The article gives no family connection to officials.
wrong.C: The article does not claim he was the only scientist of his kind.
wrong.D: His methods spread to farms well beyond one county.

questions.stem: How did Carver's approach to farming differ from the common practice of growing cotton every year?
options: Carver promoted rotating crops instead of repeating the soil
Carver avoided studying soil health entirely
Carver insisted that farmers plant cotton twice as often
Carver believed wealthy farmers should rotate crops first

wrong.B: Soil health was central to Carver's research.
wrong.C: Carver's method reduced reliance on repeated cotton planting.
wrong.D: The article does not limit his advice to wealthy farmers.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe Carver's research as both resourceful and pioneering?
options: To emphasize his inventive and far-reaching solutions
To suggest that his work was accidental and unplanned
To argue that his contributions were minor
To compare him unfavorably with other scientists
questions.why: These words highlight that Carver's solutions were both clever and among the first of their kind, addressing real problems farmers faced.

wrong.B: His years of careful experiments show deliberate, planned work.
wrong.C: The article presents his contributions as major and lasting.
wrong.D: No unfavorable comparison to other scientists is made.

HIGH.prompt: The article describes Carver's research as both resourceful and pioneering. Explain which part of his work you think mattered most and why, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I named one part of Carver's work.
I explained why I think it was important.
I supported my explanation with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think Carver's most important contribution was his sustainable crop rotation method, because it solved a problem that threatened farmers' entire livelihoods. The article explains that growing cotton repeatedly exhausted the soil of nutrients, but Carver's resourceful solution of rotating in peanuts and sweet potatoes restored the land so it could keep producing good harvests. His pioneering research into versatile new uses for the peanut then gave farmers a practical reason to keep growing it, which is why his conservation-minded approach to agriculture still matters today.
